The interpretable head of the key is amount/degree vocabulary (' handful' 1.45 in a sentence, ' plenty' 0.98, ' plethora' 0.74, ' myriad' 0.77, ' quota' 0.71, ' minority' 0.51, ' majority' 0.49, ' few' 0.39, ' subtly' 1.11, ' passionate' 0.86, ' incapable' 0.69, ' capable' 0.59, ' questionable' 0.64, ' potentially' 0.97), with a semantically unrelated tail of individual tokens and word pieces firing just as hard (' pot' 1.04, ' potato' 0.49, ' mosquito' 0.55, 'caret' 1.14, ' tasty' 1.21, ' dorm' 0.89, 'expire' 0.55, 'epad' inside ' Notepad' 1.00, 'ika' inside ' Troika' 0.63, and scattered code or control identifiers such as 'TODO', 'getArguments' and 'ObjectId' near the threshold). Because the key belongs to the token type and not to the sense, ' handful' fires in 'a handful of them' (1.45) and in 'a handful at bedtime' (1.43), ' potential' fires in 'potential energy' and ' minority' in 'the minority party', while near-synonyms that are different tokens stay silent (' modicum' 0.00, ' dash' 0.02, ' pinch' 0.20, ' numerous' 0.08, ' abundance' 0.21, ' quantity' 0.13, ' many'/' much'/' several'/' number'/' amount' <=0.12, ' meticulous' 0.05, ' esoteric' 0.02); words fire only when the Qwen tokenizer emits a high-key piece for them - the mid-sentence space-prefixed ' handful' fires, a sentence-initial capitalised ' Handful' (tokenised 'Hand'+'ful') does not, and ' Notepad' fires through 'epad' while 'capability' 0.06, 'questionably' 0.05 and 'expires' 0.19 do not. It stays at the floor (under 0.05x max) for everyday quality adjectives and for other dimensions - good, great, excellent, superb, outstanding, bad, poor, nice, fine; magnitude: important, significant, substantial, crucial, essential, major; raw potency: strong, powerful, weak, dominant; money: price, cost, rich, wealthy, expensive; social rank and honour: rank, status, prestige, respect, honour, fame, shame; emotion: angry, sad, happy, afraid; aesthetics: beautiful, ugly - so it is not an evaluation, valence, frequency or abstract-noun-suffix detector.

Check out our other articles' 1.22), and canned reader-directed idioms ('Why not try...' 1.76, 'everything you need to know' 2.15, 'How about...' 2.30, 'Here are the ten things you need to know about sleep' 0.75). It stays at baseline on the article's own sentences that carry the same words ('The meeting is on Friday, October 12, 2012' 0.42; 'Friday, October 12, 2012' embedded mid-sentence 0.28; 'All you need is in the box' 0.55 vs 'Everything you need is in the box' 1.53; 'Would you like a cup of tea?' 0.71 vs 'How about a cup of tea?' 2.30) and on short declarative site metadata ('This website uses cookies...' 0.06, 'Comments are closed.' 0.24, 'Powered by WordPress.' 0.30), so the trigger is the canned phrasing itself, not the token, the topic or second-person address. The negative pole draws the opposite contrast, firing on lively spoken-register second-person prose ('now's the time to get up and start moving' -3.07, 'We look forward to hearing from you' -2.44, 'Pleased to meet you' -1.88).

scores.explanation: The pole is a dial for plain everyday human-life prose: it accumulates over a passage of ordinary narrative or description of people and their surroundings (children, family, neighbours, homes, gardens, schools, shops, streets, food, errands) and sits near zero or below on text whose referents are technical, abstract, numeric or institutional (buffers and semaphores, enzymes and substrates, committee reports and statutes, citation strings, arithmetic drills, code). Inside such a passage it peaks on the short grammatical word that hands over to the next common noun - 'the', 'a', 'of', 'in', 'to', 'and', 'or', 'with', 'at', 'by', 'including' or a list comma - and collapses on the noun itself, and the build-up is slow, so one everyday phrase is weak while a paragraph of it is strong.

scores.explanation: Retrospective subword-fragment detector: the negative pole fires when the current token is a BPE fragment piece — a token that typically appears inside a longer word (prefix pieces like Sub/sub/subs/SUB/Fle/arbe/ery/vir/Pr/Bib/VIS/vy/fle/ple/E; mid-word pieces like ub/ry/é/erv/v) — and it fires on that token even when the word happens to end there ('a sub sandwich', 'vice versa'), while single-token words containing the same stems (obedient, subordinate, submarine, operator, virus, surgery, Troy) stay near zero and the sequence-initial token (position 0) never fires. The peak does not depend on which continuation follows ('Sub' fires ≈9.4 in Sub ordinate, Sub marine and Sub alone), and zero-ablating the pole at a peak removes next-token probability from the word's continuation pieces ('erv' after 'subs', 'ordinate' after 'ub', 'iss' after 'Fle', 'gia' after 'ry'), so its job appears to be marking 'the word is not finished' to support spelling out the rest; pieces of non-English words (arbejde, fleste, plekje, Februar) fire the same way.

scores.explanation: N2159+ is a graded-comparison detector: it fires where a quantity or degree is modified rather than stated flatly, and its sharpest peak is the second element of a reduplicated comparative ('worse and worse' 2.37, 'less and less' 1.99, 'wider and wider' 1.94, 'steeper and steeper' 1.87, 'fewer and fewer' 1.79, 'more and more of a threat' 1.64) or the junction that closes such a phrase ('the plan costs less money and takes time' peaks on 'and' at 1.81, while the same clause with 'some money' gives 0.23; 'awareness has increased only recently' peaks on 'only' at 1.90), with a weaker word-level response to the ratio and contrast markers that carry a relation themselves ('per' 0.46 and 'per cent'/'percent'/'%' 0.36-0.42 mean vs 0.06 for an average scanned token; 'rather' 0.35, 'means' 0.25, 'while' 0.24, 'yet' 0.24). It is flat on single unmodified comparatives ('buying less every year' 0.36, 'rising much faster every year' 0.09, 'more accurate than the older version' 0.22), on non-comparative reduplication ('again and again' 0.04), and on ungraded factual prose and its topic words ('university' 0.03, 'scientists' 0.03, 'said' 0.03 as preceding context), so the peak is a retrospective response to the scalar phrase it sits in, not a preparation of a specific upcoming token (zeroing the pole moves almost no probability mass: KL 5e-5, top-10 concentration 0.39, and its output direction is near-Gaussian, Jacobian kurtosis 3.7, with a below-median output norm).

scores.explanation: Retrospective detector of a possessive determiner (' their', ' his', ' her', ' our', ' your', ' my', ' its') that heads a noun phrase inside a prepositional phrase governed by the predicate - 'sent the toys to their teacher' (3.4), 'spoke with his advisors' (3.4), 'proud of their findings' (1.0), 'the sustainability of their farms' (2.9) - and it tracks that frame rather than the token: the same determiner as the verb's direct or indirect object ('sent their teacher all the toys', 0.2 vs 3.4), inside a subject-modifying or fronted PP ('To their teacher, the children gave the toys', 0.2), or an article or object pronoun in the same PP slot ('to the teacher' 0.4, 'to them' 0.1) stays near zero. Inside the PP frame the strength is graded by person/number agreement with the salient antecedent (plural subject: ' their' 3.4-4.4 vs ' his' 0.6-1.0; singular subject: ' his' 3.4 vs ' their' 1.5).
